title: Base Pairing Lets DNA Copy Itself

scenes.tts: A typical human cell with a nucleus holds nearly 2 metres of D N A. It is packed into a nucleus only about zero point zero zero five to zero point zero one millimetres across. Before a typical cell divides, it copies roughly 6 billion base pairs. It gets almost every one right. How can the structure of D N A store information and copy itself almost perfectly?
scenes.visual: A nucleus outline with a very long bar of DNA beside it, labelled nearly 2 metres, then folded inside the tiny nucleus; the 6 billion figure and the question.

scenes.tts: D N A is a long chain built from small repeating units. Each unit is a nucleotide. A nucleotide has three parts: a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group, and a base. The base carries information. D N A uses four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. We write them A, T, C and G.
scenes.visual: One nucleotide block splits into sugar, phosphate and base; units chain into a strand; four base colours with letters A T C G.
scenes.caption: DNA is a long chain built from small repeating units. Each unit is a nucleotide. A nucleotide has three parts: a sugar called deoxyribose, a phosphate group, and a base. The base carries information. DNA uses four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. We write them A, T, C and G.

scenes.tts: A covalent bond, a strong bond in which atoms share electrons, joins each sugar to the next phosphate. Two strands face each other, with their bases inside. A hydrogen bond is a weak attraction, and hydrogen bonds hold each pair of bases together. Base pairing is the rule that A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. Together the two strands twist into a double helix.
scenes.visual: Two parallel bars of blocks facing each other; backbone bonds marked, then hydrogen bonds between A-T and C-G pairs; the term double helix as a label.

scenes.tts: Because of base pairing, each strand holds everything needed to rebuild its partner. An enzyme is a molecule, usually a protein, that speeds up a reaction without being used up. One enzyme unwinds the helix and unzips it. The hydrogen bonds between the base pairs break. The backbones stay whole.
scenes.visual: The ladder unzips: the two strands pull apart, the rungs stretch and break, and each backbone stays whole; an enzyme chip at the unzipping point.

scenes.tts: Each old strand now works as a template, a pattern that sets the order of a new strand. Free nucleotides float nearby. Each one pairs with its matching base: A with T, C with G. Another enzyme, called D N A polymerase, joins the new nucleotides with covalent bonds. The result is two D N A molecules. Each has one old strand and one new strand.
scenes.visual: Free nucleotide blocks drop onto each open strand in matching order; backbones join up; two ladders, each old strand plus new strand.
scenes.caption: Each old strand now works as a template, a pattern that sets the order of a new strand. Free nucleotides float nearby. Each one pairs with its matching base: A with T, C with G. Another enzyme, called DNA polymerase, joins the new nucleotides with covalent bonds. The result is two DNA molecules. Each has one old strand and one new strand.
scenes.narration: Each old strand now works as a template, a pattern that sets the order of a new strand. Free nucleotides float nearby. Each one pairs with its matching base: A with T, C with G. Another enzyme, called DNA polymerase, joins the new nucleotides with covalent bonds. The result is two DNA molecules. Each has one old strand and one new strand.

scenes.tts: Both new molecules have the same base order as the original. So the order of the bases is the information, and copying keeps it. Base pairing allows only one correct partner at each spot. Proofreading takes out most wrong bases. A textbook estimate is about one uncorrected mistake for every billion bases copied.
scenes.visual: The two new ladders have the same colour order as the original; a one-partner check mark; a proofreading label; the one-in-a-billion estimate.
